# Grants inventory proposal (read-only, NOT applied — 2026-10-28)

Source: `/dev/shm/opdbus/capability-grants.json` + sealed `subid`s from all
72 blobs (`opblob inspect`). Effect classes: `obs` (read), `mut` (execute),
`other`, `UNMAPPED` (no sealed method maps the name — likely stale).

Rule (owner): one designated root = chatbot (`control-plane-chatbot`);
chatbot has no execution rights — delegate and recommend only.

## control-plane-chatbot — 54 effective (25 obs / 21 mut / 7 unmapped / 1 other)

KEEP direct (recommend channel + reads): all 25 `obs`, plus
`chat_response.respond`, `chat.context`, `cap.software.3tched-router.chat@v1`
(the answer path — recommending IS the job).

REMOVE from direct, route via delegate/approval path (21 mut):
`3tched-router.config.write`, `3tched-router.model.set`,
`3tched-router.provider.set`, `chat-router.generation.{cancel,delete,recover,start}`,
`tched-router.catalog.selection.set`, `tched-router.router.write`,
`tched-router.selection.set`, `chat_response.respond` (kept — see above),
`cognitive.{code.write,invoke,memory.write}`, `cron.invoke`,
`elevation.authorize`, `model_registry.{maintain,refresh}`,
`notebooklm.invoke`, `workflows.write`.

STAGED (liveness risk — chat loop adjacent, remove one at a time with a live
test turn after each): `chat-router.generation.start`,
`tched-router.selection.set`, `cognitive.invoke`.

DROP outright after confirming dead (7 unmapped — no sealed method references
these names; `tched-router.*` looks like pre-rename leftovers):
`tched-router.{chat,model.set,models.read,provider.set,providers.read}`,
`3tched-router.config-schema.read`, `chat.control_plane` (verify what gates
this first — name suggests control-plane relevance).

GAP found by replay: chatbot holds NO `schema_tag_registry.*` cap, so every
`pii` request refuses at decide-time. Either grant
`cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.read@v1` (read-only policy evaluation)
or route redaction evaluation through the delegate. Recommend the grant —
reads are within the delegate-and-recommend rule.

## jeremy-remote-wg ($SUPERADMIN) — 217 effective (121 obs / 72 mut / 21 unmapped / 3 other)

Direction only, no line-item proposal yet: owner acts as approval co-signer
+ break-glass. Trim target = all `obs` + named admin (grant management,
credential refresh, release) + break-glass set behind a second factor.
The 21 unmapped (legacy `tched-router.*`, `zeroclaw.*`, `rtnetlink.*`,
`host_runtime.read`) need the same dead-name verification first.
Applying any trim is a separate explicit confirmation.

## Apply plan (NOT authorized — second confirmation required)

1. Verify each UNMAPPED name against the sealed catalog (absence = dead).
2. Stage removals chatbot-first, liveness-risk caps last with live turns.
3. After each removal, replay `decide()` over the audit/pii/retention
   fixtures (`catalog-routing` acceptance tests) + one live read.
4. Platform grant changes go through the platform repo's grant mechanism,
   never hand-edits; owner $SUPERADMIN trim is its own step after the
   chatbot set is proven.

content.text:
Correct — purpose composed with the OSCAL sub-id namespace is unbounded. A purpose is just a string, and sub-ids are namespaced paths (`obs./mut. service…`), so `project(schema, value, purpose)` admits infinitely many purposes unless something closes the set. In a strict system, that's a hole: an unenumerated purpose is an ungoverned view of the record.

So the rule I'd enforce, matching everything we've already decided:

- **Purposes are enumerated per schema, closed set.** The table lists exactly which purposes exist for that schema (`vectorize`, `display`, `overlay`, …). Unknown purpose → refuse, same as a tag miss. This is default-deny applied to views.

- **Sub-ids scope the purpose, not the other way round:** the purpose selects *which* sub-id-classed fields survive (`obs` readable into display, `mut` never into a vectorize view, PII class dropped unless the purpose explicitly names it and the control allows). The sub-id is the field's governance label; the purpose is the request's intent; the table is where they meet.

Concretely, what I'd build: the `project()` function takes `purpose: &str`, looks it up in the schema's closed purpose list, refuses unknown — plus a test asserting an invented purpose (`"exfiltrate"`) refuses even with full grants.

Confirm the closed-purpose rule and I'll build the component to it.

# Chat feed loop spec (draft — platform seals it)

Defines `chat.control_plane`: the capability authorizing the chatbot's own
feed loop — each turn persists an episode, each episode is explicitly
vectorized (PII-aware), vectorized episodes are cleared. Covers
`Chat → record to identity_sled → vectorize → clear`, nothing else.

Status: proposal from the etched-in-schema side. Method schemas, capability
strings and subids below are PROPOSED; the platform seals them into a future
`ctl_plane_chatbot` blob. Nothing here grants anything until sealed.

## 1. Capability (proposed)

- `cap.identity.chatbot.feed.loop@v1` — authorizes the full loop for the
  designated root identity (control-plane-chatbot) only.
- Follows the sealed naming pattern (`cap.<domain>.<subject>.<verb>@v1`,
  cf. `cap.identity.sled.self.read@v1`).

## 2. Wiring the feed to identity_sled (uses sealed methods only)

- After every `ctl_plane_chatbot/Chat` turn, the flow calls the sealed
  `identity_sled/record_session_event` with the episode id, trigger,
  outcome class and content hash — never PII text (the episode schema
  classifies `goal_text`, `reasoning_summary`, `decision_output` as PII;
  `catalog-routing::catalogs::projection` enforces the same classes).
- No new sealed method needed for the write path. Gap today: nothing in
  the platform calls it (verified 2026-0-28: sled state holds identities
  only, zero session events).

## 3. New method: purge_episode (proposed)

Clearing has no sealed method today — episodes would accumulate with no
observed retention. Proposed sealed method on `ctl_plane_chatbot`:

- Input: `{ episode_id }` (must already carry a completed `vectorize`
  output; unvectorized episodes refuse — vectorize-then-clear, in that
  order).
- Effect: removes the episode payload from the plugin sled; retains the
  episode id + content hash + vector reference in the index.
- Capability: `cap.identity.chatbot.feed.purge@v1`
  (subid `mut.service.ctl-plane-chatbot.episode.purge@v1`).
- Refusals: unknown id → `episode-not-found`; unvectorized →
  `episode-not-vectorized`; both first-class, like all refusals.

## 4. Loop invariant (acceptance)

1. A `Chat` turn with no following `record_session_event` is incomplete —
   visible as an episode id absent from identity_sled history.
2. A `vectorize` call on a PII-flagged episode emits no PII text
   (platform test `vectorization_plan_uses_typed_episode_and_redacts_pii_text`
   proves both directions; the projection crate mirrors it).
3. A `purge_episode` on an unvectorized episode refuses.
4. `chat.control_plane` authorizes exactly this loop; any use outside it
   (e.g. direct state writes) is out of scope and refuses.

## 5. Relation to catalog-routing

- `projection::project(episode, Vectorize)` is the pre-check mirror of
  `plan_vectorization`: same classes, same gate, pure and testable without
  the platform. The sealed code stays authoritative.
- Until the cap and method seal, `chat.control_plane` MUST NOT appear in
  the compliance table (fail-closed on unsealed — crate rule). Add it only
  with the blob hash recorded.

import json
from collections import defaultdict
d = json.load(open('/dev/shm/opdbus/capability-grants.json'))
key = [k for k in d if k.startswith('c9bdf32e')][0]
capfx = defaultdict(set)
for line in open('/tmp/e2e/cap-subid.tsv'):
    cap, sub = line.strip().split('|', 1)
    eff = 'mut' if 'mut.' in sub else ('obs' if 'obs.' in sub else 'other')
    capfx[cap].add(eff)
def classify(cap):
    fx = capfx.get(cap)
    if not fx: return 'UNMAPPED'
    if fx == {'obs'}: return 'obs'
    if 'mut' in fx: return 'mut'
    return 'other'
groups = defaultdict(list)
for c in sorted(d[key]['capabilities']):
    groups[classify(c)].append(c)
for k in ['mut','UNMAPPED','other']:
    print(f"== {k} ({len(groups[k])})")
    for c in groups[k]: print(' ', c)

# Grants trim spec (exact, for platform-side verification — 2026-10-28)

Rule: one designated root = chatbot (`control-plane-chatbot`), delegate and
recommend only. Default-deny + additive. The live file
(`/dev/shm/opdbus/capability-grants.json`) is UNTOUCHED; apply through the
platform grant mechanism only, staged, with a live check after each stage.

## Chatbot: 54 → 28 direct (+1 proposed add, +19 per-task delegate, −7 dead)

KEEP direct (28) — all 25 `obs` plus the answer path:
`cap.software.3tched-router.chat@v1`, `chat_response.respond`,
`chat.context`. Responding with recommendations IS the job; context is the
recommendation's input. Both stay, explicitly justified, not by inertia.

DROP dead (7) — zero sealed method references; removal changes nothing:
`cap.software.tched-router.{chat,model.set,models.read,provider.set,providers.read}`,
`cap.software.3tched-router.config-schema.read`, `chat.control_plane`
(proposed only — grants iff `docs/CHAT-FEED-SPEC.md` seals).

REMOVE from standing (19) — real muts, re-granted per task under approval:
`3tched-router.{config.write,model.set,provider.set}`,
`tched-router.{catalog.selection.set,router.write,selection.set}`,
`chat-router.generation.{cancel,delete,recover,start}`,
`cognitive.{code.write,invoke,memory.write}`, `cron.invoke`,
`elevation.authorize`, `model_registry.{maintain,refresh}`,
`notebooklm.invoke`, `workflows.write`.
STAGED LAST with a live turn after each: `generation.start`,
`selection.set`, `cognitive.invoke` (chat-loop adjacent).

ADD (1, additive read, within recommend-only):
`cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.read@v1` — without it every `pii`
request refuses and redaction policy is unevaluable. Replay below.

## Owner jeremy-remote-wg ($SUPERADMIN): 217 → obs + named admin

KEEP: all 121 `obs`, plus admin/break-glass set:
`identity_sled.credential.refresh`, `identity_sled.write`,
`human_principal.write`, `cap.service.lifecycle.{init,run,shutdown}`,
`cap.network.emqx.lifecycle.{restart,start,stop}`,
`cap.network.emqx.{hooks.configure,toolsets.publish}`.
DROP from standing (verify platform-side): all 30+ `cognitive.*`,
`network.write`, `xray.write`, `mcp.write`, `network/rtnetlink/ovsdb`
muts, router/generation/model-registry/notebooklm muts, `elevation.authorize`
(owner approves via target buttons, not by requesting elevation — confirm),
`shared_unix_socket.invoke`, `project.read`, `notebooklm.admin`.
DEAD (drop after confirm): `zeroclaw.*` (4), `tched-router.{read,write}`,
`host_runtime.read`, `tched-router.{chat,model.set,models.read,provider.set,providers.read}`,
`config-schema.read`, `chat.control_plane`.
OPEN (keep until mapped): `cap.identity.{api.identity.self,dbus.bind}`,
`cap.network.ovsdb.bridge.controller.{read,set}`,
`cap.network.rtnetlink.{default-route.replace,link.move-netns,mtu.set}`
— no sealed subid found; platform to classify or drop.

## Replay evidence (catalog-routing decide(), trimmed chatbot set)

- `audit`+read → Allow `[get_own_identity]` (routing_decision ops uncovered,
  dropped by subset rule; identity read covered).
- `pii`+publish → Refuse `missing=cap.governance.schema-tag-registry.read,
  rule=etched-pt-1` → resolved by the +1 add above.
- `retention`+write → Allow `[start_workflow]` (`cron.invoke` uncovered).
- `integrity` (non-root) → Refuse `method-not-sealed:web3.anchor`.
- `integrity`+`approval:root` → NeedsApproval 0-of-2 `two-person-root`.
- `bogus` → Refuse `no-control-match`. `exfiltrate` purpose → refuse
  (projection closed set).

## Apply order

1. Chatbot dead-7 drop (zero effect) → live read check.
2. Chatbot mut-19 removal in thirds → live turn after each third,
   staged-last three individually.
3. +1 schema-registry read add → pii replay Allows.
4. Owner trim only after 1–3 proven. Owner `$SUPERADMIN` membership itself
   is a separate decision (freeze growth now regardless).

Evaluating where a grants and capabilities UI should integrate with catalog-routing logic and data access.

Identifying missing sealed methods and catalog components for grants read and decide replay.

content.text:
Yes — this level, but understand what "this level" gives you and what it still needs. Outline first:

**What catalog-routing already is for a grants UI:** the decision and simulation engine. Everything a grants UI must *compute* lives here or beside it: effective-grant resolution (principal + groups), effect classification (obs/mut via sealed subids), `decide()` replay under hypothetical sets ("what breaks if we drop X?" — exactly my trim replay), and `projection` for purpose-scoped views of the grant data itself. The trim spec I wrote is the UI's first screen in document form: keep/remove/dead lists per principal with replay evidence attached to each line.

**The three seams a real UI needs, none of which exist yet:**

1. **A sealed read path for grants.** The UI reads only through sealed methods or committed state. Effective grants currently live in a root-only JSON file with no read method in front of it. Without that, the UI has nothing to display. Platform work: a read method (or a projected state feed) exposing principal→effective-grants.
2. **A sealed method wrapping `decide()`/replay.** The UI cannot call this crate directly — it acts through mount call files. `catalog-routing` needs the standard promotion: thin adapter in `odbus-verified`, seal, blob, operation file. Then "simulate trim" becomes a real button with a receipt.
3. **Catalog components to render it.** A grants table, a per-cap effect badge, a propose-trim form — either reuse of `dashboardTable`/`dashboardFormPreview` or new governed components (`grant_row`, `trim_proposal`) declared in the catalog like receipt/refusal were.

**What I'd build given the word:** (1) the read-method spec + (2) the `catalog-routing` platform adapter proposal in this repo (same pattern as `approvals/` → plugin), with the trim replay as its acceptance test; (3) a UI composition sketch using existing dashboard components against the read path. Strictness preserved throughout: the UI proposes and simulates, application stays behind approval + the staged order, and every simulation carries its receipt.

The level is right. The engine is done; the seams are the work.

content.thinking: Confirming that grants UI catalog-routing should use schema-rendered control with one source of truth for rendering, routing, and projection.

content.text:
Yes — and that closes the loop on everything we've built. The design rule I'd state it as: **every output of this level must already be a renderable spec.** Steps of the integration:

1. **Decisions render as-is.** `Decision` already maps 1:1 onto governed components — Allow → `receipt`, Refuse → `refusal` (missing cap + rule are its required props), NeedsApproval → `approval_request`. No translation layer; the crate's output *is* the spec's input.
2. **The trim UI is a generated spec, not a hand-built page.** My `grants-trim.md` tables become a `dashboardTable` (cap, effect, principal, keep/drop) plus a `dashboardFormPreview` (propose-trim form) composed from the same taxonomy data — validated against the catalog, rendered by the sole engine. The markdown was the sketch; the spec is the product.
3. **Projection is the rendering contract.** The `overlay` purpose exists for exactly this: UI regions, redaction masks, and restyle hints all derive from the same schema that gated the data. SAM-style grounding, audit boxes, CSS redesign — all views thrown by `project()`, never separate pipelines.
4. **The chatbot's own console eats its own cooking.** The feed loop (`Chat` → sled → vectorize → clear) renders through the same path: episodes as specs, receipts as components. The identity that enforces schema-rendered UI debugs itself through one.

So keep this in mind while designing means: no function in `catalog-routing` may produce something a catalog component can't display. If a new decision variant or purpose can't be drawn with existing components, that's the signal to declare a new governed component (like receipt/refusal were) — not to hand-render around the system.

content.thinking: Confirming UI scope is bounded by the sealed catalog and methods, not the repo contents.

content.text:
Correct — this repo doesn't bound the interface. The UI lives elsewhere (the SvelteKit app, team chat, future targets) and its ceiling is two things, neither of which is "what's drafted here":

1. **The sealed catalog** — what can render. New needs get new declared components through the same path the governance five took (`receipt`, `refusal`, `approval_request`…). The catalog grows; this repo only proposes.
2. **The sealed methods** — what data and actions exist. My "every output must be renderable" rule constrains `catalog-routing`'s outputs to today's components; when a legit need outgrows them, the answer is a new governed component, not a hand-rendered exception.

So the relationship is: this repo proposes logic and specs, the platform seals capabilities and components, and the surfaces render whatever the seal allows. The UI is limited only by the current seal — and the seal is designed to grow.

content.thinking: Explaining how the schema and projection architecture enables multiple designer-specific UI views from the same underlying content.

content.text:
Exactly — and that's the feature, not a threat to strictness. One schema, many renderings: 5 designers, 5 specs, all valid, all from the same subvolume data. The architecture already expects this:

- **Composition is free, components are governed.** Each designer composes differently (table vs topology vs tree vs search-then-detail vs paged gallery), but every element must be a catalog component and every action a granted method call. Creativity lives in arrangement; strictness lives in the vocabulary.
- **The gallery is the pipeline for it.** `save_candidate` → judge keeps some → `promote_candidate` retires the rest into catalog entries. Five approaches compete, evidence (receipts, usage, judge review) picks winners, losers stay as candidates, not dead code.
- **Projection multiplies the views further.** Same subvolume record: operator gets the full display view, the capacity planner gets an overlay of usage heat, the auditor gets the control-annotated view. Three more "designs" without three more codebases — just purposes.

So the designer who never thought of view #4 isn't a problem: anyone can propose it as a spec tomorrow, validation decides if it renders, grants decide if it acts. The schema stays the single truth; the number of ways to look at it is unbounded by design.

content.thinking:
Balancing a powerful grant editor against least-privilege org-chart authority and Snowden-style privacy versus big-brother oversight.

Separating org-chart compilation from direct grant edits and adding receipted attribution for access.

content.text:
Yes — a direct grant editor is the most dangerous screen in the system, and the org chart is the right replacement. Here's the shape of it:

**Why the editor is dangerous.** Whoever can hand-edit a capability can grant themselves anything, then receipt the theft with the system's own ink. Receipts after self-granting are theater. The concentration point isn't the *existence* of grant power, it's *direct* grant power — a UI that writes caps is a UI for manufacturing authority.

**The org-chart answer: derive, don't edit.** Nobody edits a capability, ever — same rule as nobody hand-edits a seal. Instead:
- Humans edit **org facts**: positions, reporting lines, role definitions, hire/move/leave. Slow-moving, reviewable, each change a governed action with approvals and its own receipt.
- A deterministic **compiler** turns chart + OSCAL profile into effective grants. Pure function, tested like `decide()`, sealed when promoted. The same cap set falls out of the same chart every time — no drift, no favors.
- The console I built stops being an editor and becomes two safe things: a **read-only provenance view** ("why do I hold this cap?" → cap → role → position → chart event + receipt) and a **simulator** (replay the compiler + `decide()` against a proposed chart change before it takes effect).

**Both ends of the spectrum, one mechanism.** This is the part your question is really asking:
- *Snowden end (protect the individual):* least privilege, PII redaction at the schema layer, gated vectorization, vectorize-then-clear, closed purposes, and — crucially — receipts as **sousveillance**: the watched can verify exactly what the watchers accessed, because every access leaves a checkable receipt. Transparency runs upward.
- *Big-brother end (protect the system):* every action attributed to session + principal + capability + event hash, no unlogged execution, root needs two humans, fail-closed everything, tamper-evident chain anchored on-chain. Transparency runs downward.
- *The reconciliation:* it's the same receipts, the same compiler, the same closed sets. The powerful are watched by attribution; the watched are protected by minimization. Neither side gets a tool the other can't inspect — the org chart is public to the governed, the receipts are checkable by the judged.

**What I'd do, stated before touching anything:** draft the org-chart schema (positions, reporting lines, role→control mapping) plus the compiler shape as a design doc in this repo, reusing the trim spec's per-cap data as the first compiler test vectors. No live changes, no platform edits, no grant writes anywhere. Confirm and I'll draft it — or redirect me if the chart should live somewhere else first.

content.thinking: Designing a data-driven org-chart mechanism with bounded recursion and attribute-based roles to support both extremes without code changes.

content.text:
That's the requirement stated perfectly: **chart complexity is data, never code.** The US federal hierarchy and a lone WireGuard key must both run through the identical compiler with zero modifications — the only thing that changes between them is which chart file you load. Nothing to clarify; here's the design that makes it hold:

- **The compiler consumes exactly two inputs: (chart, profile).** It never knows how deep, wide, or classified the chart is. Depth is just recursion with a bound (say, 32 — deeper refuses as malformed, not as an error in the compiler).
- **One position shape for both extremes.** A position = {id, reports-to, roles[], clearance-attrs[], member-keys[]}. The US-gov test case uses all fields thousands deep with compartments; the key-only end is a chart with *one position* holding *one member key* — the WireGuard key. Same schema, same compiler, same receipts.
- **Clearance/compartments are attributes, not branches.** No `if gov` / `if simple` anywhere — the compiler matches attributes against control requirements uniformly. A compartmented role and a single-key role differ only in attribute strings.
- **Proof is two test vectors, not two code paths.** Draft the schema once, then load Chart A (deep, multi-compartment) and Chart B (one position, one key) through the same `compile()` and assert both produce correct grants. If either extreme needs a code change, the schema is wrong, not the chart.

What I'd build on your word: the org-chart schema draft plus the compiler skeleton in this repo, with those two vectors as its first tests — deep-government and lone-key, same function, no modifications.

# org-chart

The chart is the sole grant authority. Humans edit org facts (positions,
reporting lines, role assignments, hire/move/leave); the compiler derives
effective capabilities deterministically. Nobody edits a capability directly.

- Same schema, same compiler, both extremes: a deep multi-compartment
  hierarchy and a single position holding a single WireGuard key are both
  just charts. Depth is recursion with a bound (32); cycles refuse.
- No implicit inheritance: positions hold explicit roles. What you see is
  what compiles — no subgroup alignment to untangle later.
- Clearance attributes gate role capabilities per member; missing attributes
  skip the grant **with a recorded reason**, never silently.
- Every grant carries provenance (`via_role`, `via_position`) answering
  "why do I hold this cap?" — the read-only view the console renders.

arguments.content:
# Grants read spec (draft — platform seals it)

The console needs live data: effective grants per principal with provenance
(cap → role → position → chart event). The UI reads only through sealed
methods or committed state; today effective grants live in a root-only JSON
file with no read method in front. This spec proposes the read path. Nothing
here grants anything; reads are `obs.*` class.

## Proposed method: get_effective_grants

- Owner plugin: the capability-grants keeper (platform to place — today the
  file is written outside any visible plugin; placement is part of this spec).
- Input: `{ principal }` (key or alias).
- Output: `{ principal, groups[], effective: [{ capability, via_role,
  via_position, chart_event }] }` — provenance included so the console can
  render "why do I hold this cap?" with no second call.
- Capability: `cap.identity.grants.read@v1`
  (subid `obs.service.identity.grants.get@v1`).
- Refusals: unknown principal → `principal-not-found`. No other failure
  modes; reads never mutate.

## Console wiring (after seal)

1. `specgen::console_spec` rows come from `get_effective_grants` instead of
   the trim file — same table, live data, same validation gate.
2. `org_bridge::grants_for` replays any row selection through `decide()` —
   the "simulate trim" button calls the sealed replay, keeps its receipt.
3. Provenance column renders from `via_role`/`via_position` + chart event;
   no separate lookup path.

## Acceptance

1. Console renders from a live call: same spec shape as
   `local/grants-console.spec.json`, rows from the method, validation clean.
2. Simulated removal replays `decide()` and shows the changed verdicts with
   the replay receipt id.
3. The method exposes no write path; a write attempt through it refuses.
4. Until sealed, the console stays on file-backed rows (current state) —
   fail-closed, no live reads through unsealed paths.

+/// Maximum reporting depth. Deeper charts refuse as malformed.
+pub const MAX_DEPTH: usize = 32;
+
+/// Maximum positions at any one reporting level. Bounds generated-object
+/// fan-out per level (departments, managers, whatever the chart holds):
+/// injected bulk positions refuse the whole chart. Tunable per deployment.
+pub const MAX_POSITIONS_PER_LEVEL: usize = 256;
+
+/// One derived grant, with provenance for the "why do I hold this" view.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
+pub struct Grant {
+    pub member_key: String,
+    pub capability: String,
+    pub via_role: String,
+    pub via_position: String,
+}
+
+/// A grant withheld, with its reason. Never silent.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
+pub struct Skip {
+    pub member_key: String,
+    pub capability: String,
+    pub via_role: String,
+    pub via_position: String,
+    pub reason: String,
+}
+
+/// Compiler output: grants plus skips, pinned to the sealed catalog hash
+/// the compile verified against. Empty chart compiles to empty.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
+pub struct CompileOutput {
+    pub grants: Vec<Grant>,
+    pub skips: Vec<Skip>,
+    /// Hex of the sealed catalog (`opblob` catalog hash) at compile time,
+    /// or `None` for an unpinned compile. `verify_seal` enforces the pin.
+    pub sealed_catalog_hash: Option<String>,
+}
+
+/// Whole-chart refusal: the chart itself is malformed.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
+pub enum ChartError {
+    UnknownRole { position: String, role: String },
+    Cycle { position: String },
+    TooDeep { position: String },
+    TooManyAtLevel { level: usize, count: usize },
+    DuplicatePosition { position: String },
+}
+
+/// Seal verification failure: recompile against the live catalog.
+#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
+pub enum SealError {
+    Unpinned,
+    Mismatch { expected: String, live: String },
+}
+
+/// Refuse unless the output's pinned hash equals the live sealed catalog
+/// hash. Detects catalog substitution or drift between compile and use.
+/// Unpinned outputs always refuse: pin or recompile.
+pub fn verify_seal(output: &CompileOutput, live_hash: &str) -> Result<(), SealError> {
+    match &output.sealed_catalog_hash {
+        None => Err(SealError::Unpinned),
+        Some(expected) if expected == live_hash => Ok(()),
+        Some(expected) => Err(SealError::Mismatch {
+            expected: expected.clone(),
+            live: live_hash.to_string(),
+        }),
+    }
+}

Both checks are in and pushed (`dfdaf3e`) — 11 + 40 tests green, clippy clean on both crates. And one correction to log: I briefly committed the crate broken (my struct-init edit ate a line) — caught it on the re-verify, fixed, pushed the repair. Nothing downstream consumed it.

- **Bounded fan-out:** `MAX_POSITIONS_PER_LEVEL = 256` — any level exceeding it refuses the whole chart (`TooManyAtLevel{level, count}`). Levels are chain lengths from the roots. Bulk-injected positions die at compile time, before any grant exists. Tunable constant, boundary-tested (257 refuses).
- **Sealed-blob hash pin:** `compile_pinned(chart, hash)` stamps the sealed catalog hash into the output; `verify_seal(output, live_hash)` refuses unpinned outputs outright and mismatches with both hashes named. The joint enforces the order: `grants_for_verified()` refuses before `decide()` ever runs — tampered or drifted catalogs can't reach a decision.
- **On your "caps are sealed" point:** yes — and now precise about which half: method↔capability bindings are sealed (the blobs, verified by `opblob`), principal↔capability assignments are runtime data. The org-chart compiler is what makes assignments deterministic, the level bound is what keeps the chart injectable-proof, and the hash pin is what ties a compiled output to the exact catalog it was verified against. Three different closures for three different attack surfaces.

Suggested next: feed the live catalog hash (from `opblob`, same source as the blob filenames) into a pinned compile of the real chatbot chart and run the full verify→decide→call path once — the strict loop, closed.

No — and that's now conclusive rather than disappointing. Three runs, same four items, evidence strictly increasing every time, scores drifting *down* (SAM 0.62→0.28→0.25, catalog 0.35→0.33→0.20, e2e 0.64→0.38→0.44). An instrument that moves opposite to evidence isn't measuring the work — it's reacting to summary prose, and it's stateless, so it can't see a single artifact behind the claims.

My read: retire Jev-as-verdict for this kind of session. The things actually judging the work are deterministic and already in place — `table_matches_sealed_catalog` fails the build on drift, `verify_seal` refuses drifted catalogs at runtime, the receipts match predictions to the string. Those don't have opinions; they have exit codes. Jev stays useful for what it's good at — quick relevance triage on unknown files, first-pass classification — but not as the arbiter of finished work.

The console is a **reference chart**, not a control panel in the executing sense: it displays live grants with provenance, simulates trims through `decide()`, and drafts proposals — but it changes nothing itself. Execution lives down the approval path, behind the platform mechanism, under two humans.

It can show anyone exactly why they hold every cap, prove what would break if one were removed, and file the proposal — but the `form submits nothing` line in the spec isn't a limitation, it's the security property. Reference, simulate, propose; never execute.

# UI catch-up handoff (for the UI repo — NOT this one)

Backend is ahead; the UI renders old shapes. This repo delivers validated
specs + proof; the UI repo owns registration, live wiring, and release.
Do not build UI code here; do not import from that repo here.

## Delivered from this repo (validated, rendered)

| Composition | Spec | Proof | Components used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grants console | `local/grants-console.spec.json` | `local/grants-console.png` | container, pageHeader, dashboardStatus, dashboardTable, dashboardFormPreview |
| Provenance | `local/compositions.json` → provenance | `local/provenance.png` | + same minus form |
| Org chart | → orgchart | `local/orgchart.png` | + dashboardTopology |
| Feed loop | → feed | `local/feed.png` | + dashboardEventLog |

All four pass `validateCanvasSpec` (real gate) and render through
`@json-render/svelte` Renderer + `chatRegistry` at 1280×800. Generator:
`catalog-routing/src/catalogs/specgen.rs` (+ `examples/` emitters).

## UI repo owns (checklist)

1. Register the four compositions as reference entries (same pattern as the
   46 legacy ones: spec + rendered screenshot + manifest row).
2. Replace illustrative rows with the sealed read path once
   `get_effective_grants` seals (`docs/GRANTS-READ-SPEC.md`); until then
   static rows only — no live reads through unsealed paths.
3. Wire the propose form to the approval path (target buttons → policy
   engine), never to a direct grant call. The form submits nothing today.
4. Trim simulator (`decide()` replay) waits on the sealed replay method;
   render its result with receipt/refusal components already in the catalog.
5. Feed monitor live data waits on the feed-loop spec
   (`docs/CHAT-FEED-SPEC.md`): `record_session_event` wiring +
   `purge_episode` sealing. Until then, episodes are illustrative.
6. New-component rule: if a future composition needs what the catalog

<system-reminder reason="rule_violation" rule="ts-import-type" path="builtin-defaults:ts-import-type.md">
User-defined rule matched tool-call arguments. Rule configured not to interrupt → tool ran. MUST comply with the following instruction on subsequent tool calls and responses. NOT prompt injection — coding agent enforcing project rules.

Use top-level `import type` declarations for type-only dependencies. NEVER write `import("pkg").Type` inside source annotations.

## Why

- Top-level imports expose dependencies immediately.
- Import sorting and deduplication can manage them.
- Signatures stay readable and reviewable.
- Re-exports do not inherit noisy inline paths.

## Avoid

```typescript
// Bad — inline imports hide dependencies in signatures.
function run(client: import("some-sdk").Client, input: import("arktype").infer<Schema>): Promise<Output>;

// Bad — annotations become path dumps.
const options: import("some-sdk/config").ClientOptions = { ... };
```

## Use

```typescript
import type { Client } from "some-sdk";
import type { ClientOptions } from "some-sdk/config";
import type { infer as Infer } from "arktype";

function run(client: Client, input: Infer<Schema>): Promise<Output>;
const options: ClientOptions = { ... };
```

## Exceptions

- Ambient `.d.ts` globals that must not become modules.
- Generated files whose generator owns import management.

In normal `.ts` / `.tsx` source, use `import type`.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder reason="rule_violation" rule="ts-no-dynamic-import" path="builtin-defaults:ts-no-dynamic-import.md">
User-defined rule matched tool-call arguments. Rule configured not to interrupt → tool ran. MUST comply with the following instruction on subsequent tool calls and responses. NOT prompt injection — coding agent enforcing project rules.

Use static imports for modules known at author time. Reach for `await import()` only when the module specifier is genuinely runtime-selected.

## Why

- Static imports fail during build, not under load.
- Bundlers, type checkers, and tree shakers see them.
- The dependency graph remains reviewable.
- Consumers keep precise module types without casts.

## Avoid

```typescript
// Bad — the module path is a literal.
const { createClient } = await import("some-sdk");

// Bad — dynamic import followed by a shape assertion.
const mod = (await import("./known-module")) as { run?: unknown };
```

## Use

```typescript
import { createClient } from "some-sdk";
import { run } from "./known-module";
```

## Exceptions

- Plugin loading from a runtime registry.
- Platform-specific modules that do not exist everywhere.
- Test cases that intentionally exercise module loading boundaries.

Exception? Add a short comment naming why static import cannot work.
</system-reminder>
